category: Onomatopoeia and sound effects used as interjections

entries.meaning: The sound of a gunshot, a slammed door, or anything hard meeting anything hard. As an interjection it is almost always narration — you say it to replay the moment for your listener — and doubled up it is how Americans of every age imitate gunfire.
examples: He came around the corner and — bang — right into a parked car.
"Bang bang," the kid said, pointing two fingers at his brother.
I heard a bang from the garage and my heart stopped.
You slam that trunk, bang, and the alarm goes off every time.
Bang! The screen door shut behind her before I could answer.

entries.meaning: A light, hollow knock, usually on somebody's head. It is inherently comic: a bonk never really hurts and never breaks anything, so the word carries a little affection with it.
examples: He stood up too fast and — bonk — right into the cabinet door.
Bonk. She tapped him on the head with the rolled-up newspaper.
The ball went bonk off the rim and out of bounds.
I go bonk into that low doorway about twice a week.
"Bonk," my daughter said, knocking gently on my forehead. "Anybody home?"

entries.meaning: A deep explosion or a rolling, distant crash — thunder, fireworks, a demolition. It is also the all-purpose sound effect for something landing with finality, which is why people say it the moment a thing is finished or proven.
examples: There was a boom, and then every car alarm on the block went off.
You mix it, you pour it, boom — dinner's done.
Boom! The whole sky lit up green over the lake.
The transformer blew with a boom we felt through the floor.
He circled the total on the whiteboard. "And boom, there's your answer."

entries.meaning: Metal hitting metal — a dropped wrench, a cell door, a bell. The three forms are not interchangeable: a clang rings, a clank rattles, and a clunk just stops dead.
examples: The gate shut behind us with a clang.
Clang! He dropped an entire tray of pans.
Something went clunk under the hood and the car died.
You hear that clank every time the radiator kicks on.
The bell went clang clang clang and we all filed back inside.

entries.meaning: Something big breaking or falling all at once — dishes, a shelf, two cars. Dropped into a story it replays the exact instant of impact, and it is usually followed by the silence that comes right after.
examples: There was a crash in the kitchen and then total silence.
He tipped the ladder and — crash — down came the whole display.
Crash! The wind took the patio umbrella straight into the glass door.
I heard a crash, then footsteps, then nothing at all.
Every time the cat gets on the counter it's crash, crash, crash until morning.

entries.meaning: The sound of rapping on a door, said out loud instead of actually knocking — usually because the door is open or there is no door at all. It is also the fixed opening of the knock-knock joke, where it obliges the listener to answer "Who's there?"
examples: "Knock knock," he said, leaning into the doorway. "Got a second?"
Knock knock! Anybody home?
She tapped the edge of the cubicle. "Knock knock — sorry to interrupt."
"Knock knock." "Who's there?" "Boo." "Boo who?" "Don't cry, it's just a joke."
Knock knock knock on the window, and the dog lost his mind.

entries.meaning: A comic-book punch — the sound of a fist landing, printed in big letters. Americans use it for any sudden forceful hit and, by extension, for anything that arrives with a jolt.
examples: He swung and — pow — right in the jaw.
You're driving along, and pow, a deer comes out of nowhere.
Kapow! That's exactly the reaction she was going for.
One punch, pow, and the whole fight was over.
She hit the last note and pow, the entire room stood up.

entries.meaning: A flat, open-handed slap — or the wet sound of lips, whether kissing or chewing. Context settles which one you mean, and it always does.
examples: Smack! She got the mosquito on the first try.
The book landed on the desk with a smack.
He kissed her on the cheek — smack — and ran for the bus.
Please quit going smack smack with that gum.
The ball hit the wall with a smack and came right back at me.

entries.meaning: Something soft and wet hitting a flat surface — a dropped tomato, a bug on the windshield, a snowball on a wall. It is the messy cousin of thud.
examples: The egg hit the floor with a splat.
Splat! Right on the windshield, of course.
He dropped the whole scoop of ice cream — splat — on his own shoe.
The paintball caught him in the chest, splat, and the game was over.
She threw the wet towel at the wall and it landed with a splat.

entries.meaning: A light, quick knocking — on a door, a shoulder, a microphone. Said out loud, it warns someone gently that you are about to interrupt them.
examples: Tap tap. "Is this thing on?"
She went tap tap on my shoulder and I nearly came out of my chair.
"Tap tap — mind if I steal you for a minute?"
There was a rat-a-tat on the door at six in the morning.
He kept up a steady tap tap tap with his pen until I said something.

entries.meaning: A heavy, dull impact with no ring to it — a body hitting the floor, a book dropped flat, a bass drum. Thump is the same sound with a little more bounce, and it is the standard word for a heartbeat.
examples: Something hit the roof with a thud.
He fell out of the top bunk — thud — and got right back up.
I could hear my own heart going thump thump thump.
The suitcase came off the belt and landed with a thud.
Thud. The dog jumped off the couch and the whole house shook.

entries.meaning: A hard swat with something long or flat — a bat, a stick, a rolled-up magazine. Thwack adds a little sting and a little comedy; whap is the same hit landing on something softer.
examples: Whack! He caught the ball right on the sweet spot.
She hit the branch — thwack — and the snow came down on both of us.
The screen door swung back and got me, whap, right in the shoulder.
He gave the vending machine a whack and the chips came loose.
Thwack. The arrow was dead center.

entries.meaning: A sudden violent collision, almost always one nobody saw coming. It is the favorite word for telling car-accident stories and for turns of events that hit just as hard.
examples: I was stopped at the light and — wham — somebody rear-ended me.
Wham! The wind slammed the door so hard the pictures came off the wall.
Everything's fine for a year, and then wham, the rent goes up four hundred dollars.
He never even braked. Just wham, straight into the guardrail.
You take one bite and whammo, the heat hits you.

entries.meaning: A big, soft-edged impact with real weight behind it — a mattress dropped, a rotor blade, a wave against a hull. Do not confuse it with womp womp, which is a sad trombone rather than a hit.
examples: The snow slid off the roof and landed with a whomp.
Whomp! He belly-flopped straight into the deep end.
You could feel each whomp of the rotors before the helicopter cleared the trees.
She dropped the duffel bag on the bed — whomp — and started unpacking.
The waves hit the side of the boat with a slow whomp, whomp, whomp.

entries.meaning: Water falling one drop at a time. Repeated, it is the sound of a leak you cannot ignore, and it doubles as a figure of speech for anything that arrives slowly and maddeningly.
examples: Drip. Drip. Drip. I could not sleep through it.
The faucet went drip drip all night long.
There's a drip somewhere behind that wall and I can't find it.
It wasn't a flood — it was drip, drip, drip until the ceiling gave.
The story came out drip, drip, one email at a time.

entries.meaning: The hiss of carbonation — a can opening, soda over ice, a tablet dissolving. Fizzle is the same sound running out of energy, which is why it also names a disappointing ending.
examples: He cracked the can and it went fizz all over the counter.
Fizzz — that first pour over ice is the best sound in the world.
The tablet hit the water with a fizz and disappeared.
You could hear the fizz die down as it went flat.
The big finale went fizzle instead, and everybody just went home.

entries.meaning: Liquid coming out of a narrow opening in gulps — a jug emptying, a bottle being chugged. Said out loud it usually means somebody is drinking fast and you are teasing them about it.
examples: He tipped the jug back — glug glug glug.
The bottle emptied into the sink with a slow glug.
"Glug glug," she said, miming a beer. "That's his entire weekend."
You hear that glug every time the water cooler refills.
He poured the milk too fast and it came out in one long glug.

entries.meaning: A small round thing dropping into liquid, or, more loosely, anything landing without ceremony. The ker- forms are longer and funnier and put the whole fall into the word.
examples: The ice cube went plop into the glass.
He dropped his keys off the dock — kerplunk — and just stared at the water.
Plop. The frog was off the rock before anyone got a picture.
One raindrop, plop, right on the back of my neck.
The dumplings go in the pot — plop, plop, plop — and you're done.

entries.meaning: Fat hitting a hot pan. It is the sound of cooking going right, and Americans borrow it for anything with heat behind it.
examples: Butter in the pan — sizzle — and the whole house smells like Sunday.
Sssss. The steak hit the grill and nobody said another word.
You want that sizzle before you add the onions.
The rain hit the hot pavement with a sizzle and came right back up as steam.
He touched the iron and it went sizzle, and yes, it was as bad as it sounds.

entries.meaning: Something hitting water hard enough to throw it. Sploosh is bigger and sillier, and splish-splash is the light repeated version you use with a kid in a bathtub.
examples: Splash! He jumped in with all his clothes on.
The bucket went over the side with a sploosh.
You hear a splash out on the lake and you know somebody caught something.
Splish-splash — she smacked the bathwater with both hands.
A truck went by and — splash — I was soaked to the knees.

entries.meaning: A big, deliberate bite with the jaw closing hard. It is the sound of cartoon eating and of a dog taking food straight out of your hand.
examples: Chomp! The dog took the whole hot dog in one bite.
He held it up to his mouth and went "chomp chomp" like a shark.
The horse leaned over the fence and — chomp — there went my sandwich.
She took one chomp out of the apple and handed it back.
Chomp chomp chomp. That's the sound of a toddler discovering crackers.

entries.meaning: The sound of something brittle giving way — chips, gravel underfoot, frozen snow, a fender.
examples: Crunch. You could hear him eating chips over the phone.
Every step on the frozen driveway went crunch.
The bumper hit the pole with a crunch I'm still hearing.
She bit into the celery — crunch — right in the middle of the meeting.
Crunch crunch crunch through the leaves the whole way home.

entries.meaning: Swallowing hard — either a big drink or the dry swallow of somebody who has just realized they are in trouble. Standing alone in writing, a single gulp almost always means fear.
examples: Gulp. I hadn't read a single page of the assignment.
"Your mother's on the phone." "Gulp."
She looked up at the top of the ladder and said, "Gulp."
Gulp gulp gulp — he finished the whole bottle without breathing.
He saw the bill, gulp, and reached for his card anyway.

entries.ipa: /m̩ː/ (a long hum with the lips closed — no vowel in it)
entries.meaning: A closed-lip hum of pleasure, nearly always about taste or smell. Stretched out, it is a compliment to whoever cooked; the whole meaning rides on the length and the falling pitch, since there is no vowel to carry it.
examples: Mmm. That's the best thing I've eaten all year.
She took one bite and went, "Mmmmm."
Mmm — smell that. Somebody down the street is grilling.
"How is it?" "Mmm," he said with his mouth full, and gave a thumbs up.
Mmm, this coffee is exactly what I needed.

entries.meaning: Steady, unhurried chewing — snacking rather than eating a meal. Doubled, it is what people caption a picture of themselves with a bowl of something.
examples: Munch munch. Don't mind me, I found the pretzels.
He sat there going munch, munch through an entire bag of carrots.
"Munch," she texted, with a picture of the popcorn.
The rabbit worked through the lettuce — munch munch munch — without ever looking up.
I could hear you munch through that entire phone call.

entries.meaning: Happy, greedy eating, borrowed from Cookie Monster and now standard online. It is playful and a little childish on purpose: adults use it about food they are enjoying too much to be dignified about.
examples: Om nom nom. This pizza is unbelievable.
She captioned the picture of the cake "nom nom nom."
"How's the sandwich?" "Nom."
Leftover birthday cake for breakfast — nom.
Nom nom — I regret nothing.

entries.meaning: Drinking or eating noisily through pursed lips — soup, noodles, the last inch of a milkshake through a straw. At an American table it reads as bad manners, which is exactly why the word is funny everywhere else.
examples: Slurp. He got the last of it out of the straw and the whole table looked over.
She ate the ramen the right way — slurrrp — and I was jealous.
That slurp at the bottom of a milkshake is the best part of the milkshake.
The dog drank out of the toilet again — slurp slurp slurp.
Sluuurp, and the noodles were gone in about nine seconds.

entries.meaning: Said about food that looks or tastes good — before the first bite as often as after it. Yummy is the adjective form and sounds noticeably more childish coming out of an adult.
examples: Yum. Is that garlic bread?
"Chocolate chip." "Yum yum."
She looked at the menu and said, "Yum, they still have the short rib."
Yum — save me a piece of that.
"Try it." "Yummy," he said, in a voice that meant the opposite.

entries.meaning: A sneeze, written down — and also the word Americans say out loud to imitate one. A real sneeze in earshot obliges everyone present to answer with bless you.
examples: Achoo! "Bless you." "Thanks — allergies."
He went ah-choo three times in a row and gave up on the meeting.
Every spring it's achoo, achoo, achoo from March to June.
The cat sneezed — one tiny kerchoo — and looked personally offended.
She turned away from the table. "Achoo. Sorry, don't shake my hand."

entries.meaning: A deliberate throat-clearing used as a signal rather than a real cough. It asks for attention, marks that you are about to speak, or delivers a discreet correction without anyone having to say the rude part out loud.
examples: "Ahem. I believe you're in my seat."
Ahem — if anyone's counting, I finished the report an hour ago.
She gave a small ahem and the room went quiet.
"Ahem!" The teacher didn't have to say anything else.
Ahem. Some of us have been standing in this line for twenty minutes.

entries.meaning: The word said in place of the noise, usually by or about the person who just made it. Doing the real thing in public is rude in the United States; saying the word about it is a joke.
examples: Burp. "Excuse me."
He drank the whole soda and let out a burp you could hear in the parking lot.
"Burp," she said flatly, patting the baby's back. "There it is."
One sip of seltzer and it's urp for the next ten minutes.
Burp — sorry, that's just the carbonation talking.

entries.meaning: A fake cough that badly and deliberately hides a word you are pretending not to say. Written between asterisks online, it is one of the most reliable ways to be sarcastic in text; spoken, it comes out as a stage cough that fools nobody.
examples: Somebody around here — cough — never returns the stapler.
"It was a group project." "Cough cough."
He said the project was right on schedule. Cough.
The best team in the division — cough, not this year — plays Sunday.
Cough. I believe the word you're looking for is "sorry."

entries.meaning: The word for the spasm, said out loud in place of it. The short form hic is the standard way American comedy shows that a character has had too much to drink.
examples: Hic. "Excuse me." Hic. "This happens every time I eat too fast."
He wobbled in, went "hic," and everybody knew exactly where he'd been.
Hiccup. Try holding your breath and counting to ten.
"Hic — sorry, I can't stop." "Drink it upside down."
Every few seconds, hic, right in the middle of her toast.

entries.meaning: A sharp laugh out through the nose, written as a stage direction. It signals amused contempt — the thing was funny and dumb at the same time — and online it has largely taken over the job lol used to do for that reaction.
examples: Snort. Sure he did.
She read his excuse and let out a snort.
"He told them he's 'basically a doctor.'" "Snort."
Snrk — I'm sorry, I shouldn't laugh at that.
He tried to keep a straight face and it came out as a snort.

entries.meaning: The villain laugh — big, theatrical, and always at least partly a joke about being evil. Nobody has ever laughed this way by accident.
examples: "I scheduled the meeting for 4:55 on a Friday. Bwahaha."
Mwahaha! My plan is working perfectly.
He rubbed his hands together and went "bwahahaha" like a cartoon.
I ate the last of the good ice cream. Bwahaha.
"Muahaha," she typed, right after taking the last open parking spot.

entries.meaning: A single hard laugh — which, on its own, rarely means something was funny. Depending on the tone it means "I was right," "I caught you," or "that is absurd."
examples: Ha! I knew you'd say that.
"Ha. Very funny." She wasn't smiling.
Ha — you actually found it.
He read the note and just said, "Ha."
"You'll get used to it." "Ha! We'll see."

entries.meaning: Written laughter, where the length is the message: haha is polite acknowledgment, hahahaha is the real thing, and a flat ha ha with a space in the middle usually reads as sarcasm.
examples: Haha, that's a good one.
"Hahaha — okay, you got me."
She wrote back "ha ha" and I could feel the eye roll from here.
He was laughing so hard it was just ha ha ha ha into the phone.
Haha, no. Absolutely not.

entries.meaning: A fake, flat laugh that means the joke was not funny. It is always sarcastic — no one has ever genuinely laughed like this.
examples: "Har har. Very original."
He made the same short joke about my height again. Har har.
Har de har har. You should take that act on the road.
"Get it? Because you're always late." "Har har har."
She typed "har har" and then, a second later, "seriously though."

entries.meaning: A high, giggly laugh — mischief rather than comedy. Tee-hee is the same laugh with more self-awareness, usually written by an adult being deliberately cute about something small and bad.
examples: Hee-hee. I put the whole thing on his card.
She covered her mouth. "Tee-hee, sorry, I shouldn't laugh."
The kids went hee hee hee behind the couch until we found them.
"Teehee," he wrote, which is a lot coming from a grown man.
Hee-hee — wait until she sees what we did to his desk.

entries.meaning: A small, low, one-breath laugh. It means mild amusement at most, and it is very often the sound of somebody laughing at their own joke.
examples: Heh. That's actually not bad.
"Heh heh — I've done that more times than I'll admit."
He read it, said "heh," and kept scrolling.
Hehe, okay, that's funnier than it has any right to be.
"Heh." That was the entire review.

entries.meaning: The deep belly laugh, now almost entirely the property of Santa Claus. Any other time of year it reads as a deliberately hammy, old-fashioned chuckle.
examples: "Ho ho ho! Merry Christmas!"
He put on the red suit and practiced his ho ho ho in the mirror.
Ho ho — and what do we have here?
The mall Santa's ho ho ho carried all the way to the food court.
"Ho ho ho," my uncle said, handing out presents in his regular clothes.

entries.meaning: The sound of a kiss, usually one blown rather than given. It ends phone calls between family and close friends, and at the end of a text it does the work a kiss on the cheek does at the end of a visit.
examples: "Love you, honey. Mwah."
She kissed her fingers and threw it toward the stage. "Mwah!"
Thank you for the birthday flowers — mwah.
Mwah mwah — one on each cheek, and then she was gone.
"Drive safe. Muah."

entries.meaning: A loud, playful kiss — the word said instead of the kiss, or written where the kiss would go. It is warmer and sillier than mwah, and it stays inside the family and the friend group.
examples: "Smooch!" she said, and kissed the top of his head.
Thanks again for everything — smooch.
He leaned in for a smooch and the dog got there first.
Smooch smooch. Goodnight, sweetie.
"Give Grandma a smooch before we go."

entries.meaning: A short electronic tone — a microwave, a truck backing up, a car horn. Doubled, it is also how you say "move, please" from behind a steering wheel, and beep boop is the standard joke sound for a robot.
examples: The microwave went beep and nobody moved.
Beep beep! Coming through with hot coffee.
Leave a message after the beep.
The truck backed up — beep, beep, beep — for a solid two minutes.
"Beep boop, I am a robot," he said in the flattest voice he had.

entries.meaning: A low vibrating hum — a bee, a phone face-down on a table, a bad fluorescent light — or the harsh bzzt of a wrong-answer buzzer.
examples: My phone went buzz in the middle of the ceremony.
Bzzz. There is a bee in this car. There is a bee in this car.
"The capital of Australia is Sydney." "Bzzt. Canberra."
The light over the sink has a buzz I cannot get rid of.
Buzz buzz — that's the third text in under a minute.

entries.meaning: The small hard snap of a mechanism — a latch, a pen, a mouse button, a seatbelt. Clack is the harder, flatter version, and clickety-clack is a train on rails or long fingernails on a keyboard.
examples: Click. The door locked behind me and my keys were on the counter.
You'll hear a click when the car seat is in right.
He kept going click click click with that pen until somebody said something.
Clickety-clack down the hall — you could hear her heels coming.
The seatbelt went clack against the door frame.

entries.meaning: The long dry complaint of old wood or an unoiled hinge. It is the standard sound effect of a haunted house, and people apply it cheerfully to their own knees.
examples: The stairs went creak and we both froze.
Creeeak. The door opened by itself, which was the last thing I needed.
Every board on that porch has its own creak.
He got up off the floor — creak, creak — and made a joke about turning forty.
There's a creak in the hallway right where the cat likes to sleep.

entries.meaning: A single clear bell tone — an elevator, a kitchen timer, a notification. Three of them in a row means somebody has just given the right answer.
examples: Ding. The elevator opened on the wrong floor.
The oven went ding and the whole house came running.
"Ding ding ding — we have a winner."
Every time an email lands, ding, and there goes my train of thought.
The bell over the shop door went ting as she walked out.

entries.meaning: A doorbell, in its two tones. Said out loud it means "someone is at the door," or it announces that the someone is you.
examples: Ding-dong. "I'll get it."
"Ding dong! Pizza's here."
The bell went ding-dong twice and the dog lost his mind.
She knocked and then said "ding-dong" out loud, since the bell was broken.
Ding-dong — and of course there was nobody there.

entries.meaning: A long s — a snake, a leaking tire, a radiator, or a cat that has had enough. A crowd can hiss too, which is a public and old-fashioned way of booing.
examples: Hisssss. The tire was flat before we got to the highway.
The cat gave one warning hiss and left the room.
You could hear the radiator hiss all night long.
Ssss — careful, that pan is still hot.
The crowd let out a hiss when the ref made the call.

entries.meaning: A car horn — and also a goose. Said out loud, it usually reports that somebody honked at you, or that you would very much like to honk at somebody.
examples: Honk! The guy behind me had been waiting a full half second.
Honk honk — that's your ride out front.
The geese went over the field, honk, honk, all morning.
He gave one friendly little honk and waved.
One more honk out of that guy and I'm getting out of the car.

entries.meaning: An old cash register drawer flying open — the sound of money being made. Nobody uses that machine anymore, but everyone still says the sound when a deal closes or a payday lands.
examples: He signed the contract and I heard ka-ching in my head.
Two hundred a ticket, six hundred seats — cha-ching.
Ka-ching! The deposit finally cleared.
Every time they add another fee, ka-ching, straight to the bottom line.
She sold the entire set in one afternoon. Cha-ching.

entries.meaning: A small, thin, high sound — one piano key, a pebble on a windshield, a drop landing in an empty sink. Plunk is the same noise a size heavier.
examples: Plink. A single drop hit the bottom of the empty sink.
He sat at the piano going plink, plink with one finger.
The hail started with a plink on the roof of the car.
She dropped a quarter in the jar — plunk — and walked off.
Plink plink plink — the sleet was coming down on the skylight.

entries.meaning: A small sharp burst — a balloon, a cork, a knuckle, a bubble. Repeated fast, it is how Americans describe gunfire heard from a distance.
examples: Pop! The cork hit the ceiling.
The balloon went pop and the baby burst into tears.
We heard three pops and everybody hit the ground.
My knee goes pop every single time I stand up.
Pop, pop, pop — the popcorn finally got going.

entries.meaning: A telephone or a hand bell, said out loud where the sound would go. Ring ring is now faintly retro, since hardly anybody's phone actually rings anymore.
examples: Ring ring. "That's probably them now."
She held her hand up to her ear. "Ring ring — hello, reality calling."
The old rotary phone in the hall had a ring you could hear from the yard.
Brring! Nobody has ever picked up a phone faster.
Two rings and it went to voicemail, which means he declined it.

entries.meaning: A quick clean break, or a snap of the fingers. As a sound effect it marks the exact instant something gave way; as snap snap with the fingers it means "hurry up, look alive."
examples: Snap. The pencil broke right in half.
He went snap snap with his fingers and the dog sat down.
The branch went snap under my foot and every deer in the county left.
One snap of the reins and the horse took off.
Snap — that is the sound of a phone screen you cannot afford to replace.

entries.meaning: A high thin noise out of something small or unlubricated — a mouse, a sneaker on a gym floor, a hinge, a dog toy.
examples: The floorboard let out a squeak and the baby woke up.
Squeak, squeak, squeak — I got the shopping cart with the bad wheel, naturally.
Somebody's sneakers went squeak the entire second half.
Squeak! The mouse was more startled than I was.
The dog squeezed that toy — squeak squeak squeak — for forty-five minutes.

entries.meaning: A clock. Said out loud it almost never describes an actual sound — it is a way of telling somebody that time is running out on them.
examples: Tick-tock. The offer expires at midnight.
You could hear the kitchen clock going tick-tock in all that silence.
"Tick tock, people. The bus leaves in five."
Tick, tick, tick — that's the sound of your deadline.
He tapped his wrist. "Tick-tock."

entries.meaning: A plucked string letting go — a guitar, a rubber band, a bowstring. The same word names the nasal edge in a Southern or country accent.
examples: Twang. He snapped the rubber band clear across the room.
The low string went twang and the whole song fell apart.
She let the arrow go — twang — and hit the target dead center.
There's a twang in that old screen door spring every time it shuts.
Twang, twang — somebody was tuning a banjo two campsites over.

entries.meaning: A spring, or something bouncing off one — a mattress, a diving board, a coiled toy. It is a cartoon sound before it is a real one, so it always brings a little comedy with it.
examples: Boing! He hit the trampoline and went straight over the fence.
The screen door spring went sproing and came off in my hand.
Boing boing boing — the kids found the air mattress.
Her curls came loose — boing — the second she took the hat off.
The mousetrap went boing and launched itself across the counter.

entries.meaning: The sound of something vanishing in a small cloud — a magic trick, a struck match, a plan. In most real uses nothing makes any noise at all: poof is the sound of the disappearance itself.
examples: Poof. Gone. Thirty years of savings.
He snapped his fingers. "Poof — you're free to go."
The magician lifted the cloth and — poof — the bird was gone.
One rainstorm and poof, there went the entire weekend.
She said the money would just go poof, and she was right.

entries.meaning: An engine revving. Children say it while pushing a toy car; adults say it about anything moving fast, and vroom vroom is the standard tease for somebody showing off a loud vehicle.
examples: Vroom vroom — my son has been driving that couch cushion for an hour.
He revved it at the light. Vroom. Real impressive.
The bikes went by, vroooom, and set off every car alarm on the street.
"Brrm brrm," she said, running the little truck up my arm.
New exhaust, huh? Vroom vroom.

entries.meaning: Something small going past fast enough to be heard and not seen — an arrow, a bullet, a bike on the sidewalk.
examples: The ball went whiz past my ear.
Whizzz — a cyclist came out of nowhere and I nearly wore him.
You can hear them whiz by on the highway all night.
A wasp went whiz right between us and we both ducked.
Whiz, and the frisbee was in the neighbor's yard.

entries.meaning: A rush of air or a fast pass — a door opening, a bus going by, a basketball dropping through the net. Swoosh and swish are the softer, cloth-and-net versions of the same sound.
examples: The subway doors closed and — whoosh — off it went.
Whoosh! Nothing but net.
A gust came around the corner, whoosh, and took my hat with it.
He pulled the curtain back — swish — and the sun blinded everybody.
The whole afternoon just went whoosh, and now it's dark out.

entries.meaning: Electricity — a shock off a doorknob, a laser, a bug light. It also covers anything a machine does instantly, which is why Americans zap leftovers in the microwave.
examples: I touched the doorknob and — zap.
Zap! The bug light on the porch went off all night.
The fence gave the dog one little zap and he never went near it again.
Just zap it for thirty seconds and it's fine.
Zap, zap, zap — the whole laser tag arena sounded like a bad sci-fi movie.

entries.meaning: A bright singing sound — something small flying past, a struck wire — and, far more often these days, the tag somebody puts on a perfectly landed insult.
examples: "You look great. Did you finally get some sleep?" "Zing."
The arrow went zing off the metal post.
Zing! In front of his whole team, too.
She fired one right back at him and the table went, "Ooh, zing."
There was a zing in the wire every time the wind picked up.

entries.respell: bah-dum-TSS (the last beat is a hissed cymbal, not a real syllable)
entries.meaning: The drum rimshot that lands after a bad pun. It is said or typed either by the person who made the joke or by somebody else pointing out how corny it was.
examples: "I used to be a banker, but I lost interest. Ba-dum-tss."
He delivered the pun, waited a beat, and added, "Ba-dum-ching."
Somebody in the back said "ba-dum-tss" and the whole room groaned.
Badum-tss. I'll be here all week, folks.
She answered his dad joke with nothing but "ba dum tss."

entries.meaning: The three dramatic orchestra hits that follow a shocking revelation. It is nearly always ironic: you attach it to ordinary news to make it sound like a soap opera cliffhanger.
examples: "And guess who was already there? Dun dun dunnn."
It turned out the charge came from her own account. Dun dun dun.
He opened the envelope and somebody at the table went, "Dun dun duuun."
Dun dun dun — the printer had been unplugged the entire time.
She ended the story with "duhn duhn duhn" and everybody lost it.

entries.meaning: The little fanfare you sing when you reveal something you are proud of. It can be perfectly sincere or completely deadpan, and the deadpan version is funnier.
examples: She pulled the cake out of the box. "Ta-da!"
Ta-da. Two hours of work and it still looks like a pancake.
He fixed the sink, wiped his hands, and said, "Ta-daa."
Ta-da — one working printer, exactly as promised.
"Close your eyes. Okay, open them. Ta-da!"

entries.meaning: The sad trombone — the sound of failure, played over somebody's disappointment. Aimed at yourself it is self-deprecating; aimed at someone else it is a small and very cheerful cruelty.
examples: "They gave the promotion to Dave." "Womp womp."
Sold out. Wah-wah.
I drove all the way out there and they'd closed at four. Womp womp.
He missed the shot and the whole bench went "wah wah waaah."
"Womp womp," she said, and somehow I felt worse.

entries.meaning: A sheep. It lives in picture books and petting zoos, and it gets borrowed for people who follow the crowd without thinking about it.
examples: "What does the sheep say?" "Baa!"
The lambs went baa every time we walked past the fence.
Baaa — one of them answered him right back.
He held up the toy sheep and said, "Baa, baa, black sheep."
Everybody just repeats whatever the boss said. Baa.

entries.meaning: A small bird, a cricket, or a smoke detector with a dying battery. Said into a silence after your own joke, chirp chirp is the cricket gag: nobody laughed and you know it.
examples: Chirp, chirp — the birds started before the sun did.
I made the joke and the room went dead quiet. Chirp. Chirp.
The smoke alarm gave one chirp every ninety seconds all night.
"What does the bird say?" "Tweet tweet!"
Out past the porch light it was nothing but cheep, cheep, cheep.

entries.meaning: A rooster. It is the standard American version of the crow, learned in early childhood, and adults use it to mean "it is unreasonably early" or "get up."
examples: "And what does the rooster say?" "Cock-a-doodle-doo!"
Cock-a-doodle-doo! Everybody up — we leave in ten minutes.
The rooster next door starts his cock-a-doodle-doo at 4:45 sharp.
He threw open the curtains and yelled "cockadoodledoo" at his sleeping teenager.
Cock-a-doodle-doo — out there, that's the only alarm clock anybody has.

entries.ipa: /ɡr̩/ (a growled *r* with no vowel in it)
entries.meaning: A growl. Out of a dog it is a warning; out of a person it is a small, half-joking noise of frustration, and it is much milder than actually saying you are angry.
examples: Grrr. The website logged me out again.
The dog gave a low grr and I put the treat back in the bag.
"How'd the meeting go?" "Grr."
Grr — I missed that train by about ten seconds.
She typed "grrrr" and then, a second later, "okay, I'm over it."

entries.meaning: An owl. American children learn it as hoo, hoo, and the sound is shorthand for night, woods, and everything being very quiet.
examples: Hoo, hoo. There's an owl in that tree every single night.
"What does the owl say?" "Hoot hoot!"
We heard one long hoot and then nothing for an hour.
Who-who — he did the owl call and one actually answered him.
The barn owl's hoot carried all the way across the field.

entries.meaning: A cat. Said by one person about another, it flags that somebody just made a catty, claws-out remark.
examples: The cat sat by the empty bowl going meow, meow, meow.
"She called his new place 'charming for the price.'" "Meow."
Meow! Somebody's in a mood this morning.
"What does the kitty say?" "Meow!"
A tiny mew came from under the porch, and that is how we got Charlie.

entries.meaning: A cow. It is a barnyard-and-toddler word through and through, and one of the first sounds American children are taught to make.
examples: "What does the cow say?" "Moo!"
One moo from the far end of the field and the whole herd answered.
Mooooo — he did the cow voice and the baby laughed for ten minutes.
We drove past the dairy and the kids yelled "moo" out the window.
Moo, moo. The toy makes the sound every time you tip it over.

entries.meaning: A horse. Children say it; adults imitating a horse usually skip the word and do the whinny instead.
examples: "What does the horse say?" "Neigh!"
She galloped around the yard going "neigh, neigh."
Neighhh — he did the horse voice and the pony ignored him completely.
The horse let out a long neigh the second the feed bucket came out.
Every toy in that barn set goes neigh when you press it.

entries.meaning: A pig. Outside the barnyard, saying oink oink at somebody is a small insult about greed or table manners.
examples: "What does the pig say?" "Oink oink!"
The pigs at the fair went oink the second they saw the bucket.
He took the last three slices. "Oink."
Oink oink — that's the sound of a man double-dipping.
She squeezed the toy pig and it went oink about four hundred times.

entries.meaning: The rumble of a contented cat. Said of an engine it means the thing is running beautifully; said of a person it means they are being openly pleased with themselves.
examples: One scratch behind the ears and it was purrrr for the rest of the movie.
Purrr. That is the sound of a cat who got exactly what she wanted.
New timing belt, and now the engine just goes purr.
"Purr," he said, admiring his own parking job.
You can feel the purr before you can hear it.

entries.meaning: A duck. It mostly stays at the pond and in picture books, though quack quack also does duty for somebody talking on and on about nothing.
examples: "What does the duck say?" "Quack quack!"
The ducks came right up to the bench — quack, quack, quack — expecting bread.
Quack! His duck call sounded almost real.
He held up the rubber duck and made it go quack.
Twenty minutes of quack quack quack and he still hadn't gotten to the point.

entries.meaning: A big animal roaring — a lion, a dinosaur, a monster in a game of pretend. Spelled rawr it is playful and slightly flirty; spelled roar it is the actual animal.
examples: Rawr! He came around the corner as a dinosaur and the toddler screamed with joy.
"What does the lion say?" "Roar!"
She sent back a "rawr" and I still don't know how to read it.
Rawr — that's my monster voice and it is terrifying.
The crowd let out a roar when he came out of the tunnel.

entries.meaning: A frog. It is the standard American frog sound, even though only some frogs actually make anything like it.
examples: "What does the frog say?" "Ribbit!"
Ribbit, ribbit — the pond behind the house is loud all summer.
He hopped across the room going "ribbit" and the kids followed him.
One ribbit out of the reeds and then total silence.
Ribbit ribbit. The sound machine has an entire swamp setting.

entries.meaning: A dog. Woof is the deep bark, arf and ruff are the small ones, and bow-wow is the storybook version children meet first.
examples: "What does the doggy say?" "Woof woof!"
Arf! The little one barks at absolutely everything.
He knocked on the door and got exactly one woof in reply.
Bow-wow — that's the entire first page of the book.
She barked back at him. "Ruff." The dog was not impressed.
